Title: This is university work
Search words: expected, expectations, expect, standard, university, uni, level 7, aqf, bachelor, first year, elective, easy, hard, difficult, workload, hours, how much work, how many hours, time, effort, high school, not high school, serious, credit points, what is expected
Decides: What the marks in this course are for, and what they are not for.
Start with: Read this once, before you start the report. Then use the section pages as you work.
Do this:
This is a level 7 course, which means a bachelor degree standard. It is the same standard whether marketing is your major or this is an elective, and it is higher than school.
Marks are for analysis and decisions: what the evidence shows, why it matters for your brand, and what you decided because of it. Facts and descriptions on their own earn few marks.
A table is your working. The section is the writing. A filled table with no paragraphs under it is an unfinished section.
Every claim has a source you can cite, from the list on the assessment page. If you cannot cite it, leave it out.
Each section uses a decision from the one before it. Read your report backwards and you should see the chain.
Plan on about nine hours a week: three in class and six of your own. The report is built across the semester from the weekly activities, not written in the last week.
Your tutor shows you where to look and how to think about it. The decisions and the writing are yours.
The rules are not optional. Late is late, the word count is a maximum, and AI is allowed only where the assessment page says so. Check them before you start.
Watch out:
Treating a first year course as small. It carries the same credit points as the other courses in your degree, and the report is marked to the same standard.
Doing the activity sheets and stopping. The sheets give you the evidence. The report is where you use it.
Leaving the writing to the last week. The sections depend on each other, so the last week cannot fix the first.
Goes next: Every section page in this guide has the same shape: what the section decides, what to do, the table and the writing, what to watch out for, and where it goes next.
Taught in: Week 1, and the assessment pages in Canvas.

Title: Company and brand today (1.1 to 1.3)
Search words: section 1, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, company, brand owner, parent company, portfolio, brands, brand today, mission, vision, market share, brand performance, five years, what the brand sells, starting point
Decides: What the brand brings to a new category: who owns it, how big it is, and whether it is growing or shrinking.
Start with:
The brand named in the brief.
The owner's website and annual report, and market data for the brand's current category.
Do this:
1.1 Introduce the owner: who owns the brand, how long it has operated in this market, its mission or vision, and what it sells here. Cite each fact.
1.2 List the owner's main brands in this market and the categories they compete in.
1.2 Give the owner's market share in the brand's current category, with the basis (value or volume) and the year.
1.2 Write two or three things you notice in the portfolio that matter for an extension, such as a premium or value focus, health claims or heavy discounting. Give evidence for each.
1.3 Describe what the brand sells now, with a labelled product image and its source. Give its market share and whether it has grown, declined or stayed stable over five years.
1.3 In four or five sentences, say what this performance means for its ability to extend: trust, relevance, distribution strength, competitive pressure. Link each point to evidence.
Table and writing: No table is required. Figures go in sentences with citations, and any image is labelled. Each fact ends with why it matters for the extension.
Watch out:
A fact with no citation earns no marks, even when it is true.
A description with no 'so what' is not analysis. Every fact should matter for the extension.
Market share with no basis (value or volume) and no year cannot be checked.
Goes next: Section 2 uses the owner's size and position. Section 7 draws strengths and weaknesses from here. In Assessment 3, Section 2.2 maps this brand's product mix.
Taught in: Week 2, Tutorial Activity 1. Theory Map: brand audit.

Title: The extension opportunity (2.1 and 2.2)
Search words: section 2, 2.1, 2.2, industry, industry analysis, current industry, future industry, extension industry, adjacent industry, benchmark, key players, top five, growth, outlook, drivers, trends, compare industries
Decides: Which industry the brand should extend into, and why the move is worth making.
Start with:
Passport industry reports for the brand's current industry and for the industry you want to enter.
One adjacent industry to use as a benchmark, measured the same way and over the same years.
Do this:
2.1 Define the current industry: what is in it and what is not. Name the top five companies and their main brands, including the brand owner.
2.1 Show five years of performance and the outlook for the next five, with the drivers behind the change. Keep one measure (value or volume) throughout.
2.1 Compare its growth with the adjacent industry, so the reader can tell whether growth is low, moderate or high.
2.2 Do the same for the future industry: definition, top five companies and brands, five years back, five years ahead, drivers, adjacent benchmark.
2.2 Compare the two industries side by side: growth, main competitors, trends and drivers. Then say what the brand gains and risks by moving from one to the other.
Table and writing: The working notes table from the Week 2 activity is for the tutorial, not the report. The section is paragraphs that compare the two industries and end with what the brand gains and risks.
Watch out:
Two separate descriptions are not a comparison. The marks are in the connection between them.
A growth figure on its own says little. The adjacent industry is what gives it meaning.
Mixing value and volume, or different years, makes the comparison invalid.
Goes next: Section 3 narrows the industry to one category. Section 7 draws opportunities and threats from here.
Taught in: Week 2, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: brand extension and equity transfer, industry analysis.

Group: Section 3: The new category and its competitors
Title: The new category and its competitors (3.1 and 3.2)
Search words: section 3, 3.1, 3.2, category, new category, choose category, product category, product segment, segment, competitors, competitive set, direct competitors, indirect competitors, private label, category rules, deep dive, top three, crowded
Decides: The one category and the one product segment the brand will enter, and who it will compete with there.
Start with:
Your future industry from Section 2, and the category rules on the assessment page.
Passport category and segment data.
Do this:
3.1 List and define the categories in your future industry, using the structure your sources use.
3.1 Deep dive the top three: five years of performance, five year outlook, drivers, key brands and their owners, and how crowded each one is.
3.1 Compare the three on size, growth, outlook, brands and competition. Choose one and justify it with evidence. Name one or two risks.
3.2 Repeat the same steps for the product segments inside your chosen category. Recommend one segment as the best opportunity.
Name the competitive set for that segment: the direct competitors, the indirect ones, and private label where it matters.
Check your category against every rule on the assessment page before you go further.
Table and writing: You may design a comparison table for the body. The decision is a paragraph: which category and segment, the evidence, and the risk.
Watch out:
If your category breaks a rule on the assessment page, every section built on it is affected. Check the rules first.
Product segments are about products, not people. Consumer segments come in Section 6.
A choice with no risks named reads as a guess. Markers look for the risk and how you weighed it.
Goes next: Every section after this is about this category. Section 4 analyses its environment, Section 6 its shoppers, Section 7 its SWOT and objectives. Assessment 3 builds the plan for it.
Taught in: Week 2, Tutorial Activity 2 (the working notes table), and Week 3. Theory Map: category and segment analysis, competitor analysis.

Title: Micro environment
Search words: section 4, 4.1, micro, micro environment, microenvironment, actors, company, suppliers, intermediaries, marketing intermediaries, competitors, publics, customers, findings, so what, close to the business
Decides: Which close to the business actor matters most for competing in your category, and what it changes.
Start with:
Your chosen category from Section 3.
The six actors: company, suppliers, marketing intermediaries, competitors, publics, customers.
Do this:
For each of the six actors, find at least three findings from the required sources. Write each as one full sentence: what is happening, the evidence, and the so what.
Keep the worksheet tables in the appendix, with the name of who found each point.
Choose the one actor with the biggest effect on competing in your category.
Write one short paragraph on that actor: why it matters most right now, using at least two of your findings. End with one sentence on the main marketing impact: product, price and promotion, distribution, or how you compete.
Write the body of the section in paragraphs, not bullet points.
Table and writing: The six worksheet tables go in the appendix. The body is paragraphs: a summary of the findings and one paragraph on the actor that matters most. No bullet points in the body.
Watch out:
A topic is not a finding. 'Suppliers' says nothing. 'Supply costs for the main ingredient rose by X per cent since Y' does.
Findings about the brand in general, not your category, do not count.
Business, government and international markets are outside this course. Leave them out of customers.
Goes next: Strengths and weaknesses in Section 7 come from here and from Section 1.
Taught in: Week 3, micro environment activity. Theory Map: micro environment.

Title: Macro environment
Search words: section 4, 4.2, macro, macro environment, macroenvironment, forces, six forces, demographic, economic, natural, technological, political, cultural, trends, pestle, outside world, demand, costs, competition
Decides: Which outside force matters most for your category, and whether it changes demand, costs or competition.
Start with:
Your chosen category from Section 3.
The six forces: demographic, economic, natural, technological, political, cultural.
Do this:
For each force, find at least three trends from the required sources. Write each as one full sentence that makes sense on its own, with a citation.
Make each one a trend, something changing over time, not a fact that sits still.
Keep the worksheet tables in the appendix, with who found each trend.
Choose the one force that matters most for your category right now. Write one short paragraph using at least two of its trends.
End with one sentence on the main effect on the market: demand (what sells), costs (what it costs to operate) or competition (who you compete against).
Table and writing: The six worksheet tables go in the appendix. The body is paragraphs: a summary of the trends and one paragraph on the force that matters most. No bullet points in the body.
Watch out:
Macro forces are things the company cannot control. If the company can change it, it belongs in the micro environment.
A trend with no source is an opinion, and opinions earn no marks.
Six forces means six. Leaving one out leaves a gap the SWOT cannot fill.
Goes next: Opportunities and threats in Section 7 come from here and from Sections 2 and 3.
Taught in: Week 3, macro environment activity. Theory Map: macro environment.

Title: Consumer and market analysis
Search words: section 5, consumer analysis, market analysis, interviews, interview, primary research, three questions, three people, nine interviews, questions, survey, ask people, what people said, summary
Decides: What real shoppers told you about your category, as the evidence your segments rest on.
Start with:
Your chosen category.
The segment each member is researching. No two members research the same one (Section 6 says how segments are chosen).
Do this:
Each member writes three questions about buying and using the category, for the segment they are researching.
Each member asks their own three questions to three people who fit their segment. A group of three does nine interviews.
Write a short summary of what the interviews found: the patterns, not every answer.
Put the questions and the answers in the appendix.
Carry what you learned into your own segment column in Section 6, and cite the interviews there.
Table and writing: The questions and answers go in the appendix. The body is a short summary of the patterns, in paragraphs.
Watch out:
Questions about the brand are not questions about the category. Ask about buying and using, not about liking the brand.
Three people is a small sample. Report what they said as what they said, not as what everyone thinks.
A summary that repeats each answer in turn is not analysis. Group what you heard.
Goes next: Section 6 uses this as evidence for the behavioural rows of the matrix. The Assessment 3 persona draws on it too.
Taught in: Week 4. Theory Map: consumer and market analysis.

Title: Segmentation (6.1 and 6.2)
Search words: section 6, 6.1, 6.2, segmentation, segments, segment, matrix, segmentation matrix, geotribes, geosmart, abs, demographics, geographics, psychographics, behavioural, criteria, five criteria, measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable, actionable, criterion paragraph, 100 words, segment name, legend
Decides: Which groups of shoppers exist in your category, and what makes each one different from the others.
Start with:
Your Section 5 interviews.
The required profiling sources: RDA GeoTribes, RDA GeoSmart and the ABS.
The matrix template from the Week 4 activity.
Do this:
As a group, give each member a different GeoTribes segment. No two members use the same one.
Each member fills every row of their own column: demographics, geographics, psychographics and behaviour. Bullet points in the table. Give the segment a name of your own, not the GeoTribes or GeoSmart name.
Fill the behavioural rows from your interviews and your category research: brands bought, where they shop, occasion, frequency, benefits sought, loyalty, attitude, media.
Reference inside the table with a legend, and list the full references in the reference list.
6.2 Each member writes one paragraph of no more than 100 words that shows the segment is measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable and actionable, and says how it differs from the other segments in the group.
Paste the matrix into the body of the report as a Word table, not an image.
Table and writing: The matrix goes in the body as a Word table. It is not the section on its own: each column needs its 100 word criterion paragraph.
Watch out:
A segment described only by age and gender is not differentiable. Psychographics and behaviour are what make it distinct.
Every row must be filled. An empty row is a gap the persona cannot fill later.
Where they shop and the media row matter later. The persona, the retailer choice and the media plan in Assessment 3 all read from these rows.
Goes next: Section 7 draws on the segments. In Assessment 3, your own segment becomes your persona, so build the column you will want to work from.
Taught in: Week 4, Tutorial Activity 1. Theory Map: market segmentation, segmentation criteria.

Title: SWOT
Search words: section 7, 7.1, swot, strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, quadrant, boxes, five to six points, control, prioritise, decide, no new information
Decides: Which one fact from your analysis matters most, and whether the brand should act on it or protect against it.
Start with: Sections 1 to 6. The SWOT contains nothing new.
Do this:
Collect the facts from Sections 1 to 6 that matter most for the extension. For each one ask: can the company control it?
Yes and it helps: a strength. Yes and it hurts: a weakness. No and it helps: an opportunity. No and it hurts: a threat.
Write five or six points in each box. Strengths and weaknesses come from Sections 1 and 4.1. Opportunities and threats come from Sections 2, 3 and 4.2.
Put the most important point first in each box, so the SWOT shows what you have prioritised.
Pick the one point that matters most and say what the brand should do about it. That decision leads to your objectives.
Table and writing: The SWOT grid goes in the body with five or six points in each box. Under it, a paragraph names the point that matters most and what the brand should do about it.
Watch out:
A point that appears for the first time in the SWOT is new information. Markers check for it, and it is not allowed.
Opportunities are outside the company. 'Launch a new flavour' is an action, not an opportunity. 'Demand for X is growing' is one.
Four boxes of equal weight hide the decision. A SWOT that does not prioritise reads as a list.
Goes next: 7.2 turns the point you chose into objectives. In Assessment 3, the opportunity you chose becomes the position (Section 1.3).
Taught in: Week 5, Tutorial Activity 1. Theory Map: SWOT analysis.

Title: Marketing objectives
Search words: section 7, 7.2, objectives, objective, marketing objectives, smart, smart objective, share objective, sales objective, market share, sales, value, volume, basis, workings, two objectives, goals, targets
Decides: What the extension must achieve in its first period, as two numbers the plan can be measured against.
Start with:
Your SWOT decision.
Market size and share data for your new category from Passport.
Do this:
Write two objectives for the new category: one market share objective and one sales objective.
Make both SMART: a number, a basis (value or volume), the category, and a date.
Use the same basis for both. Value with value, or volume with volume.
Show the workings behind each number in the appendix: the category size, the share you expect, and where the figures came from.
Check each one with the SMART test in the Week 5 activity. Circle Yes or No for each letter.
Table and writing: The workings go in the appendix. The body states the two objectives and says, in a sentence each, where the numbers came from.
Watch out:
A tactic with a number is not an objective. 'Run a campaign in March' is a tactic. 'Reach X per cent share of the category by a date' is an objective.
Objectives for the brand's current category are the wrong objectives. These are for the extension.
A number with no workings cannot be checked, so it earns nothing.
Goes next: In Assessment 3, the advertising objective (5.2) and every media target (5.4) must sit under these two objectives: smaller and earlier.
Taught in: Week 5, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: marketing objectives (SMART).

Title: Does it all connect?
Search words: connect, connected, link, links, flow, consistency, joins, together, whole report, overall, one argument, read backwards, three threads, thread, structure, high mark, hd, distinction
Decides: Whether the report reads as one argument, from the brand today to the objectives.
Start with: Your finished draft. Read it backwards, from Section 7 to Section 1.
Do this:
Our objectives (7.2) come from the SWOT point we chose (7.1).
Every SWOT point can be traced to a sentence in Sections 1 to 6.
Our segments (Section 6) are shoppers in the category we chose in Section 3, not in the brand's current category.
Our interviews (Section 5) show up in the behavioural rows of the matrix.
The competitive set in Section 3 is the one Section 4.1 analyses.
The industry we chose in Section 2 is the one our category in Section 3 sits in.
What the brand stands for (Section 1) explains why it has permission to enter the category (Section 3).
Table and writing: Every table in the report has sentences next to it that say what it shows and what it changes.
Watch out:
Three members writing three sections each produces three reports. Read the whole thing together once before you submit.
If a section changes a decision made earlier, say why in one sentence, or the marker will read it as a mistake.
Goes next: Assessment 3 carries three things over: your segment becomes the persona, your SWOT opportunity becomes the position, and your objectives sit above every target.
Taught in: Weeks 2 to 5. Assessment 2 Theory Map: the three threads.

Title: Before you submit
Search words: ready, ready to submit, submit, final check, checklist, before submitting, before i submit, proofread, finished, done, upload, turnitin, file name, word limit
Decides: Whether the report is ready to upload.
Start with: The assessment page open beside your report.
Do this:
Section numbers and headings match the assessment page.
Every claim has a citation, or workings in the appendix.
Our sources follow the rules on the assessment page, and no banned source appears anywhere in the report.
Our AI declaration is in the appendix, even if we used none.
The matrix is a Word table, not an image, and the worksheet tables are in the appendix.
We are under the word limit. The executive summary, contents, reference list and appendix do not count.
The file name matches the pattern on the assessment page, and one member uploads it early.
Every table has writing next to it that says what it shows.
Table and writing: A filled table with nothing written under it is an unfinished section. Check every table before you upload.
Watch out:
Even five minutes late is a full day late, for every member.
Nothing sent by email is marked.
Goes next: After results, read the comment in each rubric row. Assessment 3 starts from this report.
Taught in: The Assessment 2 page in Canvas.

Title: Target market (consumer persona)
Search words: section 1, 1.1, persona, consumer persona, target market, target segment, day in the life, goals, motivations, pain points, media consumption, brand relationships, template, one page, landscape, table, needs, barriers, drivers, triggers
Decides: Who the plan is for: one real feeling shopper drawn from your group's segment.
Start with:
Your own segment column from the Assessment 2 matrix, and your interviews.
The persona template and rules in the Week 6 activity document.
Do this:
Build one persona from the segment you built in Assessment 2. If your Assessment 2 feedback told you to change segment, say so in one sentence.
Fill every part of the template. Go past age and income to needs, barriers, drivers and triggers in your category.
Write the day in the life around the category: when they use it, with whom, and what the moment is for.
Name the brands they buy in the category and the relationship: loyal, occasional, switching.
Say where they shop and what media they use. Sections 4 and 5 read these two lines.
Keep every format rule in the Week 6 document: a table on one page, not an image, not made in a design tool.
Table and writing: The persona is the one section where the table is the section. No written explanation is required, so every cell must be specific to your category and your segment.
Watch out:
A persona built from general facts about an age group does not lead to decisions. The needs do.
Goals, pain points and motivations must be about the category, not about life in general.
The format rules are part of the mark.
Goes next: The persona's main need sets the core benefit (2.3). Where they shop sets the first retailer (4.1). Their emotion sets Feel (5.3). Their media line sets the channels (5.4).
Taught in: Week 6, Tutorial Activity 1. Theory Map: Section 1.

Title: Positioning map
Search words: section 1, 1.2, positioning map, map, perceptual map, axes, axis, variables, white space, bubbles, bubble size, market share, competitors on the map, four brands, three competitors, direct competitors, low to high
Decides: The white space in the market your brand can own, on two axes that matter to your persona.
Start with:
Your persona's needs and motivations (1.1).
Market share for your brand and its direct competitors, from Assessment 2 and Passport.
The map template and rules in the Week 6 activity document.
Do this:
Pick two axes from your persona's needs, motivations or usage occasions. Each runs from low to high.
Plot your brand and at least three direct competitors. Your persona decides who counts as direct: the brands they would choose between.
Size each bubble by market share. Put the share workings and the Passport source in the appendix.
Name the white space: the position no brand fully delivers that your persona values.
Place your brand in that space on purpose, and write a few lines on why you chose the two axes.
Use the template and add shapes. Do not paste the map as an image.
Table and writing: The map goes in the body, with shapes on the template, plus a few lines on why you chose the axes. The share workings go in the appendix.
Watch out:
Price, quality and taste are not allowed as axes. They apply to every brand and show nothing.
An axis you cannot trace to a line in your persona is the wrong axis.
Bubbles all the same size mean the share step was skipped.
Goes next: The white space becomes the key benefit in your statement (1.3). The product (2.3) and the advertising (5.3) must deliver this position.
Taught in: Week 6, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: Section 1.

Title: Positioning statement
Search words: section 1, 1.3, positioning statement, statement, formula, point of difference, swap test, key benefit, need, target segment, one sentence, slogan, tagline
Decides: One sentence that says who the brand is for, what need it meets and why it is different.
Start with:
Your persona (1.1), your map (1.2) and your group's SWOT opportunity from Assessment 2.
The formula in the Week 6 activity document.
Do this:
Fill every part of the formula: the segment, the need, the brand, the category, the key benefit.
Take the segment from your Assessment 2 matrix, the need from your persona, and the benefit from the white space on your map.
Make the point of difference claim the opportunity your group chose in its SWOT.
Run the swap test: put a competitor's name in place of yours. If the sentence still works, sharpen the benefit until it does not.
Write one statement only. It is a strategy sentence, not a slogan.
Table and writing: One sentence in the body. The swap test is your check, not a paragraph.
Watch out:
A statement that would fit any brand in the category has no point of difference.
If the segment, need and benefit do not line up with your persona and map, fix the earlier work rather than rewording the sentence.
Goes next: Everything after this must deliver this sentence. The product (2.3), the price level (3.1) and the big idea (5.3) all say the same thing in their own form.
Taught in: Week 6, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: Section 1.

Title: Product strategies (product life cycle)
Search words: section 2, 2.1, plc, product life cycle, life cycle, stage, introduction, growth, maturity, decline, category stage, five years, passport value, table b, placement, product strategy, costs, profits
Decides: What stage the category and each competitor are at, and so what kind of launch this is.
Start with:
Five years of Passport value data for your category.
The competitor set from your map (1.2).
Do this:
Set the category's stage from five years of value data. Sales decides the stage. The other rows should mostly agree.
Place your brand and three competitors on the life cycle, each on its own, with a reason.
Write costs and profits as what theory expects at that stage, not as facts, because they are not published for one brand.
Place your new product at Introduction, even when the category is mature. A new product always starts there.
Put the first two PLC tables in the body and Table B (the placement summary) in the appendix. Then state the product strategy that fits the stage.
Table and writing: Two PLC tables in the body, Table B in the appendix. Under the tables, paragraphs: the stage, the reason, and the product strategy for that stage.
Watch out:
A stage with no five year data behind it is a guess, and markers check the data.
Mixing up the category stage and the product stage is the most common error here. They are usually different.
Tables are not in the word count, so there is no reason to leave them out.
Goes next: The stage drives skimming or penetration (3.1), distribution intensity (4.1), the promotion mix (5.1) and the objective type (5.2).
Taught in: Week 7, Tutorial Activity 1. Theory Map: Section 2.

Title: Product mix
Search words: section 2, 2.2, product mix, mix, width, length, depth, lines, product lines, range, before and after, new line
Decides: Where the new line sits in the brand's range, and what the range looks like after launch.
Start with: The brand's current range, from Assessment 2 Section 1.3 and the brand's own website.
Do this:
Map the brand named in the brief, not the parent company and not the category.
Show width (how many lines), length (how many products across them) and depth (versions of each) before the new line.
Add the new line and show the mix after launch. Count the existing lines. Write out only the new line in full.
Explain what changes, and why it fits what the brand stands for.
Table and writing: The mix can be a table, before and after. Under it, a paragraph on what changes and why it fits the brand.
Watch out:
Mapping the parent company's whole portfolio answers a different question.
Depth means versions of one product (sizes, flavours, packs), not a list of everything the brand sells.
Goes next: Where the new line sits shapes the price level and the price steps inside the line (3.1).
Taught in: Week 7, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: Section 2.

Title: Total product concept
Search words: section 2, 2.3, total product concept, total product, three layers, core, actual, augmented, core benefit, hero product, hero image, product image, labelled image
Decides: What the hero product is, in three layers, and which layer carries the persona's main need.
Start with: Your persona's main need (1.1) and your positioning statement (1.3).
Do this:
Choose one hero product from the new line.
Core: the benefit the shopper is really buying. It must answer your persona's main need.
Actual: the product itself. Brand name, pack, format, features and quality level.
Augmented: what comes with it. Guarantee, service, extras.
Include a labelled image of the hero product with its source. Say what carries over from the parent brand and what is new.
Table and writing: The three layers can be a table or a labelled figure. Each layer needs a sentence that links it: the Core to the persona's need, the Actual to the brand, the Augmented to what the shopper gets.
Watch out:
Being stocked by a retailer is a Place decision (Section 4), not an Augmented element on its own.
A core benefit that does not answer the persona's need breaks the join from Section 1.
No image, or an image with no label and source, loses the easy marks.
Goes next: The core benefit becomes the benefit line in 5.3. The Augmented layer informs the price level (3.1).
Taught in: Week 7, Tutorial Activity 3. Theory Map: Section 2.

Title: Pricing strategies
Search words: section 3, 3.1, price, pricing, pricing strategies, price level, skimming, penetration, customer value, cost based, competition based, goods type, convenience, shopping, specialty, unit price, shelf price, price steps, launch price
Decides: How the price level is set, and whether the launch skims or penetrates.
Start with:
Your PLC stage (2.1), your position (1.3), your product mix (2.2).
The retailer's unit prices for your competitors.
Do this:
Say how the price level is set: customer value, cost or competition based. Give the reason.
Choose skimming or penetration. Argue it from the textbook conditions, the PLC stage, the position and the persona.
Check the goods type: convenience, shopping or specialty. It shapes both the price and the distribution later.
Compare your shelf price with competitors using the retailer's unit price, so the comparison is like for like.
Show the price steps inside the new line, from your product mix.
Table and writing: The price comparison is a table in the body. The decisions are paragraphs: the approach, skimming or penetration and why, the goods type, the price steps.
Watch out:
A price with no method behind it cannot be defended. Name the approach first.
Skimming at Introduction in a crowded category needs a strong reason. Say what it is, or choose penetration.
Comparing pack prices of different sizes is not a comparison. Use unit price.
Goes next: The goods type and the stage set the distribution intensity (4.1). The price level sets the room for the tactic in 3.2.
Taught in: Week 8, Tutorial Activity 2. Theory Map: Section 3.

Title: Promotional pricing strategies
Search words: section 3, 3.2, promotional pricing, promotional price, price tactic, tactic, discount, specials, competitor prices, price history, price trend, screenshots, depth, how often, launch offer, rejected option
Decides: The one short term price tactic for launch, chosen against what competitors already do.
Start with:
Your persona (1.1) and your competitors (1.2).
